newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU rule on D.Telekom cable in March- report.
newsitem.headline: EU rule on D.Telekom cable in March- report.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert is expected to present the findings of a study in March that could result in forcing Deutsche Telekom to divest all or part of its cable television network, a German magazine reported on Tuesday.

Deutsche Telekom is so concerned about the Commission's findings that chief executive Ron Sommer plans to meet behind closed doors with German parliament's postal affairs committee, the monthly Capital magazine said.
The European Commission, under the direction of Van Miert, is conducting a study on the impact of the possession of cable television networks by former telecommunications monopolies.

The study will explore whether, as in Germany, ownership of such networks by dominant carriers after liberalisation of European telecommunications next year would impede competition and what might be done further competition.
Van Miert has in the past taken a critical view of Deutsche Telekom's ownership of Germany's only cable television network.

According to a pre-release of a report in the upcoming issue of Capital, the Commission is currently discussing three alternatives to weaken Telekom's dominance of the German telecommunications market.
-- Force Telekom to divest the network altogether.
-- Place the network into a separate company and not allow Telekom to hold more than 25 percent of the new company.
-- Break up the network into regional cable companies.

Last year the Commission forced Dutch telecoms operator KPN to sell its cable television network to further competition. In the rest of Europe, only in Germany and Portugal do former telephone monopolies also have a cable television monopoly.

Deutsche Telekom until last year had a monopoly on ownership of cable television networks in three of the four so-called network levels. Competitors were only allow to hook up individual homes to Deutsche Telekom's trunk network.
As a result, while Telekom owns the only national trunk cable TV network in Germany, it only has 5.5 million of the more than 16 million cable TV subscribers under direct contract.

The remaining cable TV customers subscribe to regional services, such as those offered by Vebacom GmbH, the joint venture between Veba AG and Cable and Wireless, which with nearly two million cable TV subscribers, is Germany's second-largest cable TV operator.

A conflict of interest has emerged between Telekom and the regional operators. While companies like Vebacom want to use the cable TV network for basic phone services, Deutsche Telekom is blocking this by declining to make the necessary technological upgrade of the existing cable network.
Telekom's competitors say this is exactly the reason why the Commission should get involved to weaken Telekom's grip on the cable television network.
